concept.name: Perplexity-Based Token Pruning & Entropy Context Compression
concept.title: Perplexity-Based Token Pruning & Entropy Context Compression
concept.tagline: Compressing 128k–1M token prompts 8x–64x down to 8k–16k tokens in <120 ms while preserving >98% of entities and reasoning invariants.
concept.purpose: Understand why naive recency truncation breaks agent tool schemas and safety rules, and how Small Language Model (SLM) conditional perplexity scoring paired with Pinned Anchors and query-contrastive PMI preserves factual density.

prerequisites.title: Shannon Information & Token Surprisal
prerequisites.summary: Know that a token's information content is I(x_i) = -log2 P(x_i | x_<i): predictable boilerplate carries near-zero bits, while rare entities and constraints carry high surprisal.

prerequisites.title: Transformer Prefill & KV-Cache Scaling
prerequisites.summary: Understand that a 70B FP16 GQA-8 model consumes ~160 KB of KV cache per token, meaning 1M tokens requires 160 GB of GPU HBM.

spark.summary: Partition prompts into immutable Pinned Anchors (system prompts, tool schemas, safety rules) and compressible context, then prune low-surprisal tokens using a quantized 0.5B–1.5B SLM conditioned on the active user query.
spark.keyTakeaway: When 128k–1M token agent contexts blow up prefill latency and KV-cache memory, pin system prompts and tool schemas as immutable anchors and prune only low-perplexity filler tokens with query-aware SLM scoring so >98% of entities survive.
spark.byteSummary:
Feeding 250,000 to 1,000,000 raw tokens into a frontier LLM on every agent turn burns 15–35 seconds of prefill time and up to 160 GB of FP16 KV cache on a 70B model. Worse, naive recency truncation—keeping only the last 16k tokens—silently drops system instructions, JSON tool schemas, and early user constraints.

Perplexity-based token pruning, pioneered by Microsoft Research's LLMLingua and LongLLMLingua, exploits the massive redundancy of natural language and tool logs. First, deterministic boundary rules lock Pinned Anchors (system prompts, OpenAPI schemas, safety invariants) with infinite priority so they are never modified. Next, a fast quantized 0.5B–1.5B Small Language Model (SLM) scores the remaining compressible chunks in parallel, computing conditional surprisal I(x_i) = -log2 P(x_i | x_<i) plus a query-contrastive PMI boost.

Low-surprisal filler tokens ('please note that', repetitive JSON keys, verbose prose transitions) are pruned while high-entropy entities, numbers, error codes, and causal verbs are kept—shrinking 1M tokens down to 8k–16k tokens in <120 ms with >98% entity preservation.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & Why Naive Context Truncation Fails
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows why sliding-window truncation destroys tool schemas and why raw 1M prefill hits an HBM wall.

explanation.foundation: A 70B LLM with GQA-8 uses ~160 KB of FP16 KV cache per token. At 1M tokens, a single session needs 160 GB of KV cache—exceeding an 80 GB H100—and takes ~18–35 seconds just to prefill before emitting token #1.
explanation.core: If you naively truncate to the last 16k tokens, you amputate the system prompt, JSON tool definitions, and early API keys or user constraints—causing immediate tool-call schema failures and safety regressions.
explanation.deepDive: Even when a model supports 1M-token context natively, 'lost-in-the-middle' attention dilution degrades multi-hop entity recall compared to a dense, high-signal 12k-token prompt.

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: Pinned Anchors & Conditional Surprisal
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Separates zero-tolerance structural anchors from entropy-prunable narrative and log tokens.

explanation.foundation: Every prompt is partitioned into Class A Pinned Anchors (system prompt, tool schemas, safety invariants, pinned facts) with weight w = infinity, and Class B Compressible Segments (RAG passages, tool stdout, old turns).
explanation.core: For Class B tokens, a 0.5B–1.5B INT8 SLM computes conditional surprisal I(x_i) = -log2 P(x_i | x_<i). Tokens the SLM predicts with >95% probability carry <0.07 bits of information and are safe to drop; unexpected tokens (UUIDs, latency numbers, stack traces) carry 6–12 bits and are kept.
explanation.deepDive: To protect tokens that look locally predictable but matter to the active question q, LongLLMLingua adds a query-contrastive PMI term: S(x_i | q) = I(x_i) + alpha * [PPL(x_i | x_<i) - PPL(x_i | q, x_<i)].

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant & Safe Python Implementation
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Demonstrates anchor-protected quantile thresholding with 128-token stride overlap.

explanation.foundation: A critical implementation bug when scoring 1M tokens in parallel 4k chunks is boundary perplexity inflation: token 0 of every chunk has no left context, so its surprisal spikes artificially.
explanation.core: The fix is a 128-token overlap stride between adjacent 4,096-token chunks, discarding scores from the first 64 tokens of chunk k > 0 (only ~3.1% compute overhead) before running O(N) threshold selection.
explanation.deepDive: Pinned anchors are concatenated at a fixed prefix offset before compressed segments, preserving >85% GPU RadixAttention prefix-cache hit rates across multi-turn agent loops.

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: Hierarchical Trees & KV Eviction
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Combines perplexity pruning with bottom-up summarization trees for 50+ turn agent sessions.

explanation.foundation: Token-level perplexity pruning excels at 8x–20x compression, but 1M -> 8k (125x) needs structural abstraction over old turns.
explanation.core: Aging 4k-token leaves are asynchronously distilled into 512-token branch summaries and a 128-token root spine, while H2O Heavy-Hitter Oracle retains attention sinks (indices 0..7) and high-attention tokens in GPU HBM.
explanation.deepDive: Each 512-token branch keeps a rehydration pointer [ref:leaf_id] so if a later query references an old detail, the assembler fetches the raw 4k leaf from NVMe RocksDB in <8 ms.

decisionFramework.title: Choosing Compression Strategy by Target Ratio
criteria: 2x–10x ratio: Pure query-aware SLM perplexity pruning (preserves verbatim IDs & code).
10x–64x ratio: Pinned Anchors + SLM perplexity on recent/relevant chunks + 512-tok tree summaries on old turns.
Latency > 450 ms: Trip Fail-Open Circuit Breaker to Pinned Anchors + last 12k raw tail tokens.

decisionExercise.prompt: An agent coding session has 180k tokens of old build logs plus a 2k-token JSON tool schema, and p95 SLM scoring latency spikes to 470 ms. Which action protects both correctness and SLO?

options.label: Drop the 2k JSON tool schema to free budget
options.feedback: Dropping tool schemas causes malformed tool calls and immediate agent failure.

options.label: Trip the 450 ms fail-open breaker: emit Pinned Anchors + 12k raw tail
options.feedback: Correct: failing open preserves the 500 ms SLO while keeping tool schemas and recent turns intact.

options.label: Run a 70B LLM synchronously to summarize the 180k logs
options.feedback: A 70B synchronous summary adds 10–20 seconds and worsens the latency breach.

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions, When NOT to Use & Glossary
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Establishes strict operational boundaries, failure modes, and terminology.

explanation.foundation: Assumptions & Limitations: Assumes an 8k–16k target window, quantized 0.5B–1.5B SLM workers co-located with LLM inference pods, and deterministic anchor delimiters.
explanation.core: When NOT to Use It: Do not run perplexity pruning on short <8k prompts (adds unnecessary 90 ms overhead), cryptographic/legal verbatim contracts where single-word omissions alter liability, or dense minified code where every symbol has high entropy.
explanation.deepDive: Glossary: Pinned Anchor (w=inf immutable block), Conditional Surprisal (-log2 P(x_i|x_<i)), Query-Contrastive PMI (query-relevant boost), Boundary Stride Overlap (128-token chunk fix), H2O Heavy-Hitter (cumulative attention KV retention), Fail-Open Breaker (450 ms fallback to raw tail).

sectionDiagram.title: 450 ms Compression Circuit Breaker State Machine

steps.label: 1. Anchor Extract
steps.detail: Lock 1.8k tokens of System Prompt + Tool Schemas (SHA-256 verified) in 3 ms.

steps.label: 2. Parallel SLM Score
steps.detail: Split 248.2k tokens into 62 x 4k chunks (128 overlap); INT8 0.5B SLM scores in 95 ms.

steps.label: 3. Quantile Prune
steps.detail: Select top 10.2k high-surprisal tokens via tau threshold; assemble 12k prefix-stable prompt.

steps.label: 4. Shadow Audit
steps.detail: 5% async judge confirms 98.7% NER & numeric fact retention.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must system prompts and JSON tool schemas be locked as Pinned Anchors before perplexity pruning?

options.text: Because SLM perplexity is higher on JSON braces
options.feedback: Boilerplate JSON keys often have low perplexity and would be pruned.

options.text: Because pruning structural keys or safety rules breaks tool execution and safety invariants
options.feedback: Correct: Pinned Anchors receive w=infinity so 0% of schemas or safety rules are dropped.

options.text: To disable GPU KV-cache prefix reuse
options.feedback: Fixed-offset Pinned Anchors actually maximize KV-cache prefix reuse.
Anchors are compact (1k–3k tokens) and protect correctness.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Deterministic JSON schemas and safety rules cannot tolerate even 1% token loss; pinning them at a fixed prefix also enables RadixAttention KV reuse.

knowledgeChecks.question: How do you eliminate artificial perplexity spikes at the start of parallel 4,096-token scoring chunks?

options.text: Score all 1M tokens sequentially on one GPU
options.feedback: Sequential scoring violates the <500 ms p95 latency budget.

options.text: Use a 128-token overlap stride and discard scores from the first 64 tokens of chunk k > 0
options.feedback: Correct: overlap provides left-context at only 3.1% compute overhead.
BM25 drops semantic connectors and reduces entity recall to ~86%.

options.text: Drop the first 500 tokens of every chunk
options.feedback: Dropping 500 tokens blindly would lose real facts.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A 128-token overlap stride gives the SLM proper left context for boundary tokens.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens when the 450 ms compression circuit breaker trips to OPEN?

options.text: All agent requests fail with HTTP 503
options.feedback: Failing closed degrades platform availability unnecessarily.

options.text: The gateway fails open by emitting Pinned Anchors + the last 12k raw tail tokens
options.feedback: Correct: failing open keeps the <500 ms p95 SLO and preserves tool schemas.

options.text: It routes to a 70B LLM summarizer
options.feedback: A 70B summarizer is much slower than the 0.5B SLM.

options.text: It clears Redis L1 across all tenants
options.feedback: Clearing Redis L1 would cause a massive state miss storm.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Fail-open degradation ensures context compression never becomes an availability bottleneck.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why sample 5% of turns to an async Shadow LLM Judge instead of running it synchronously?

options.text: Sync LLM judging would add 800+ ms and double inference cost, violating the <500 ms p95 SLO
options.feedback: Correct: async 5% sampling calibrates threshold tau with zero hot-path latency.

options.text: Kafka cannot carry JSON payloads synchronously
options.feedback: The bottleneck is LLM judge latency and GPU cost, not Kafka.

options.text: Shadow judges only run on failed requests
options.feedback: It samples 5% of successful compressed turns to detect fact drift.
Shadow auditing respects tenant HMAC isolation.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Async shadow auditing gives closed-loop recall telemetry (>98% SLA) with zero p95 latency penalty.

beginner.summary: Keep important instructions locked at the top, and use a tiny fast model to trim repetitive filler words from huge prompts.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When prompts get too big and slow, lock your rules and schemas first, then let a small model trim low-value filler.
beginner.byteSummary: Large AI prompts waste time and GPU memory on repetitive words. By locking system rules as Pinned Anchors and using a tiny 0.5B model to keep only high-information words, you shrink 1M tokens to 12k in under half a second.

intermediate.summary: Partition context into immutable Pinned Anchors and compressible chunks, scoring tokens in parallel with an INT8 0.5B SLM and query-aware PMI.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When 128k–1M token prompts exceed latency budgets, score 4k chunks in parallel with a 128-token overlap stride and prune below quantile threshold tau.
intermediate.byteSummary: Parallel SLM perplexity scoring measures conditional surprisal across 4k chunks with a 128-token overlap stride to avoid boundary spikes. Combined with query-contrastive PMI and a 450 ms fail-open breaker, it sustains >98% entity recall.

advanced.summary: Combine deterministic SHA-256 Pinned Anchors, chunk-parallel INT8 SLM surprisal + query PMI, RAPTOR-style summary trees, H2O KV eviction, and a 5% async shadow PID controller.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When compressing 1M-token multi-tenant agent contexts under 500 ms p95, co-design fixed-offset Pinned Anchors for RadixAttention reuse with parallel SLM pruning and async tree distillation.
advanced.byteSummary: At 1,000 turns/sec (250M raw tok/s), 62 parallel 4k chunks per turn are scored in 90 ms (L=90 concurrent turns across 32–40 INT8 GPUs), cutting 70B FP16 KV cache from 160 GB to 1.92 GB per session while a 5% shadow judge tunes tau to hold >98% entity recall.
